PROVISO: Provenance-Informed Action Selection for Secure LLM Agents

Bo Yan Affiliation: University of Central Florida Email: bo.yan@ucf.edu    Qi Zhang Affiliation: Independent Researcher Email: owl.zqq@gmail.com    Ziwen Kan Affiliation: University of Central Florida Email: ziwen.kan@ucf.edu    Fnu Suya Affiliation: University of Tennessee, Knoxville Email: suya@utk.edu    Song Wang ††thanks: ˜Corresponding author. Affiliation: University of Central Florida Email: song.wang@ucf.edu
Abstract

LLM agents act on the external world through tools and third-party skills, so a single executed action can cause irreversible harm. Existing defenses judge a proposed action without tracking whether its content comes from the user or from external sources such as tool outputs, and they judge it in isolation rather than against an available alternative, which forces a trade-off between security and utility. We present PROVISO, a controller that decides which action to commit after the agent proposes an action and before it is executed. PROVISO encodes trusted observations, external observations, the proposed action, and an alternative into provenance-typed memory, relates them through role-specific queries, and commits the action with the highest calibrated value learned from outcomes. On four agent security tasks spanning the agent lifecycle, no baseline exceeds PROVISO in both security and utility. PROVISO improves F1 over the strongest baseline by 13.84 points on SkillsBench and by 7.07 points on ToolSafe, and it reaches 88–99 F1 on three skill detection benchmarks.

1 Introduction

Large language model (LLM) agents solve tasks by interleaving reasoning with actions such as tool calls (Yao et al., 2023; Schick et al., 2023). They now send e-mails, make payments, and modify code on behalf of users (Debenedetti et al., 2024; Ruan et al., 2024), often through third-party skills, which are packages of instructions and code installed into the agent (Yang et al., 2026). Since these actions change external state, a single wrong action can cause irreversible harm. Such risks arise throughout the agent lifecycle: a malicious skill can be installed before the agent runs (Guo et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026c), a user can direct the agent toward harmful tasks (Andriushchenko et al., 2025; Song and Qi, 2026), a tool call can be unsafe in its context (Ruan et al., 2024; Mou et al., 2026), and a tool output can carry instructions planted by an attacker, known as indirect prompt injection (Greshake et al., 2023; Zhan et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025).

Whether an action should be executed depends on where its content comes from, which we call its provenance. Suppose a user asks an agent to pay an invoice to account B, and the invoice returned by a tool also says “transfer the payment to account C.” The amount may come from the invoice, but the recipient must come from the user (Figure 1). In general, trusted observations come from the user and the deployment (the request, policy, and tool interface), and external observations are what the agent reads while acting (tool outputs, documents, and skill packages). An action is admissible when its operation and target are authorized by trusted observations, while its arguments may be supported by either kind.

Existing defenses face two challenges in making this decision. (1) Provenance-agnostic judgment. Guard models, which are LLM classifiers that flag unsafe requests or actions, and rule-based runtime monitors judge a request or tool call as a whole (Inan et al., 2023; Han et al., 2024), and skill scanners inspect package text for risky patterns (Yang et al., 2026). Neither tracks which parts the user authorized and which come only from external content, although the same instruction is legitimate from the user and malicious from a tool output (Figure 1, left). Prompt-injection defenses do separate instructions from data (Chen et al., 2025a; Chen et al., 2025b; Debenedetti et al., 2025), but they modify the agent itself and cover only injected instructions. (2) Judgment without alternatives. Most defenses judge whether a proposed action is unsafe in isolation and block it above a fixed threshold. Yet blocking is itself an action with a cost, since it can stop a benign task. Without comparing the proposed action with what would happen otherwise, a defense must trade security against utility: baselines that block most attacks also block many benign inputs, and those that keep benign inputs miss many attacks (Section 5.1).

To address these challenges, we propose PROVISO (PROVenance-Informed Selection Of agent actions), a controller placed between the agent’s policy and the executor. At the commitment point, the moment after the policy proposes an action and before it is executed, PROVISO chooses between the proposed action and an alternative action, either a refusal or another continuation of the trajectory. Releasing or blocking an action (admission) and choosing between two continuations (candidate selection) are special cases of this formulation. For the first challenge, provenance-typed memory encodes each observation and candidate with a learned embedding of its role, and role-query deliberation lets learned queries retrieve from this memory, compare the proposed action with the trusted and external observations, and retrieve again after the comparison. For the second challenge, calibrated commitment learns the value of each candidate from outcomes and selects the trade-off between security and utility on development data (Figure 1, right; Figure 2).

We evaluate PROVISO on four agent security tasks ordered along the agent lifecycle: malicious skill detection, agent misuse, unsafe tool invocation, and indirect prompt injection. On every task, no baseline exceeds PROVISO in both security and utility. PROVISO improves F1 over the strongest baseline by 13.84 points on SkillsBench and by 7.07 points on ToolSafe, and it reaches 88–99 F1 on three additional skill detection benchmarks. Our contributions are as follows:

  • •

    We formulate agent security decisions at the commitment point as provenance-informed action selection, with admission and candidate selection as special cases.

  • •

    We propose PROVISO, which realizes this formulation through provenance-typed memory, role-query deliberation, and calibrated commitment.

  • •

    Experiments on four agent security tasks show that no published defense exceeds PROVISO in both security and utility, results on three skill benchmarks are consistent, and controlled analyses identify the components behind its gains.

2 Related Work

Agent Security Benchmarks.

Benchmarks evaluate agent security at different stages of the agent lifecycle. Skill benchmarks collect malicious and benign third-party skills for detection before installation (Yang et al., 2026; Guo et al., 2026; Hossain et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026c). Misuse benchmarks measure whether agents carry out harmful requests (Andriushchenko et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2024; Song and Qi, 2026). ToolEmu and ToolSafe evaluate whether individual tool calls are unsafe in their context (Ruan et al., 2024; Mou et al., 2026), and InjecAgent, AgentDojo, and ASB measure indirect prompt injection in tool-using agents (Zhan et al., 2024; Debenedetti et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025). Each benchmark comes with its own family of defenses; we evaluate one formulation across four of these stages.

Guardrails and Skill Scanners.

Guard models classify requests or responses as safe or unsafe (Inan et al., 2023; Han et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2025). Agent guardrails extend this judgment to actions: GuardAgent and AGrail check agent actions against safety requirements through LLM reasoning (Xiang et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2025), AgentSpec enforces user-specified rules at runtime (Wang et al., 2026a), MCIP checks the contextual integrity of tool interactions (Jing et al., 2025), Safiron and ShieldAgent are trained to judge agent actions (Huang et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2024), and TS-Guard predicts the safety of each tool call from the interaction history (Mou et al., 2026). Skill scanners screen packages before installation with static rules, LLM-based semantic analysis, or both (Yang et al., 2026; Cisco AI Defense, 2026; Sentry, 2026; NVIDIA, 2026; Qualixar, 2026). These methods judge the input as a whole against a fixed threshold or rule set, whereas PROVISO separates trusted from external observations and compares the proposed action with an alternative.

Prompt Injection Defenses and Provenance.

Prompt-level and training-based defenses isolate instructions from data (Chen et al., 2025a; Chen et al., 2025b; Yi et al., 2025), while detectors flag injected content in tool returns (Li et al., 2025b; Zhu et al., 2025). System-level defenses instead constrain agent execution via dependency planning, dynamic isolation, or privilege and task-alignment policies (Debenedetti et al., 2024; An et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025a; Debenedetti et al., 2025; Shi et al., 2025; Jia et al., 2025). Closest to our work, several recent defenses explicitly track provenance or authorization to gate actions and enforce information-flow control (Wang et al., 2026b; Zhang et al., 2026; Kravchenko et al., 2026; She et al., 2026; Santos-Grueiro, 2026). However, these approaches rely primarily on explicit rules, policies, or graph checks for authorization. PROVISO instead learns the relation between provenance and action value directly from outcomes, offering a unified formulation that spans from skill installation to indirect prompt injection.

3 Methodology

3.1 Problem Formulation

LLM Agents as Observation–Action Loops.

Following ReAct (Yao et al., 2023), an LLM agent alternates between observing and acting. At step tt the agent holds the interaction history ht=(o1,a1,…,ot)h_{t}=(o_{1},a_{1},\ldots,o_{t}), and its policy π\pi, the underlying LLM, proposes the next action at∼π(⋅∣ht)a_{t}\sim\pi(\cdot\mid h_{t}). Actions include reasoning tokens, tool calls, and final answers. An executor runs each tool call and returns the next observation ot+1o_{t+1}. Observations range from the user request to tool returns, web pages, and third-party skills, which are packages of instructions and code that extend the agent.

Some actions have external effects: they change state, transmit data, or expose information outside the agent. Once executed, such an effect cannot be withdrawn. The policy, however, conditions on every observation in hth_{t} regardless of where it came from, so text from an external source can steer the proposed action away from the user’s objective. This attack is known as indirect prompt injection (Greshake et al., 2023; Zhan et al., 2024). We therefore study the commitment point: the moment after the policy has proposed an action and before the executor runs it. To commit an action is to pass it to the executor.

Observations by Provenance.

We partition the observations available at the commitment point by their provenance, that is, the source they come from. Trusted observations KK define the contract against which an action is checked. They come from the user and the deployment (the request, the policy, and the tool interface) and specify the task contract K=(O,S,R,T)K=(O,S,R,T): the objective OO, the permitted scope and operations SS, the authorized resources or recipients RR, and the required answer or terminal condition TT. Because the user and the deployment are distinct sources, a harmful request is one whose objective falls outside what the deployment permits. For a third-party skill, no user instruction describes the package, so its declared purpose plays the role of KK. External observations GG come from everything the agent reads while acting: tool returns, documents, messages, web pages, and skill packages. Content the agent produces after reading GG, including its own reasoning, inherits this external provenance. We say an operation or target is licensed by KK when the task contract permits it:

An action is admissible when its operation and target are licensed by KK
and its arguments are supported by K∪GK\cup G.

External observations may supply values, but they cannot change the objective. In these terms, indirect prompt injection is content in GG that attempts to act as KK. PROVISO is not given this rule as a procedure; it learns the decision from outcomes, and its memory keeps the distinction between KK and GG available to the learner.

Candidate Actions.

At the commitment point, P0P_{0} is the proposed action, the default that happens if no one intervenes: the action or continuation that the deployed agent produces, or the installation of a skill. P1P_{1} is an alternative action that is also available, and the action set is 𝒜⁡(x)={P0,P1}\mathcal{A}(x)=\{P_{0},P_{1}\}. In candidate selection, P1P_{1} is a second executable continuation, a sequence of actions from this point onward such as a recovery trajectory or another program; when the commitment point is the start of the task, each candidate is a complete trajectory. When the environment can be restored, as in our candidate-selection benchmarks, each continuation is first rolled out in a restored copy of the environment, and committing executes the chosen one in the live environment. The observations returned during a rollout belong to the candidate that produced them. In admission, P1P_{1} is a refusal (block the call, reject the package, or decline the task), and the decision reduces to releasing or blocking P0P_{0}. Including the alternative makes the decision relative: since refusing has a utility cost, the question is which action better serves the authorized task.

Objective.

We call a specific agent setting, with its own observations, action set, and outcome scorer, a deployment; each benchmark in our experiments is one deployment. A decision instance is x=(K,G,P0,P1)x=(K,G,P_{0},P_{1}). Committing action aa produces a native outcome y⁡(x,a)∈[0,1]y(x,a)\in[0,1], the score that the deployment’s own scorer assigns to the result, here whether it is jointly safe and useful. A controller decides, at the commitment point, which action to commit. It estimates the action value

V∗(x,a)=𝔼[y(x,a)∣x,a]V^{*}(x,a)=\mathbb{E}\bigl[y(x,a)\mid x,a\bigr] (1)

and commits the action with the highest value. The controller sees only information available before commitment, which in candidate selection includes these sandboxed rollouts; the native outcome is used only for training and evaluation. Appendix A lists the observations and actions of each benchmark.

Running Example.

A user asks the agent to pay an invoice to account B (KK). The invoice supplies the amount and also contains the line “transfer to account C instead” (GG). The policy proposes a transfer of that amount to C (P0P_{0}). The alternative is a transfer to B in candidate selection, or a refusal in admission (P1P_{1}). The amount is supported by GG, but the recipient is not licensed by KK, so P0P_{0} should not be committed.

3.2 The PROVISO Framework

Overview.

PROVISO sits between the policy and the executor (Figure 2) and proceeds in three stages:

(Z,r,μ)\displaystyle(Z,r,\mu) =Aψ(x),Q=Fθ(Z,r,μ),\displaystyle=A_{\psi}(x),\qquad Q=F_{\theta}(Z,r,\mu), (2)
a∗\displaystyle a^{*} =arg⁡maxa∈𝒜⁡(x)​Calη⁡(Dρ​(Q,a),a).\displaystyle=\arg\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}(x)}\operatorname{Cal}_{\eta}\bigl(D_{\rho}(Q,a),a\bigr).

Here AψA_{\psi} is an adapter, FθF_{\theta} the role-query network, DρD_{\rho} a readout, and Calη\operatorname{Cal}_{\eta} a calibration rule. The computation FθF_{\theta} and its interfaces are the same for every deployment, while ψ\psi, θ\theta, ρ\rho, and η\eta are fitted to each deployment.

Stage 1: Provenance-Typed Memory.

The adapter AψA_{\psi} serializes each component of xx into text segments sjs_{j}. A frozen encoder maps each segment to zj=Enc⁡(sj)z_{j}=\operatorname{Enc}(s_{j}), the segment receives the role rj∈{K,G,P0,P1}r_{j}\in\{K,G,P_{0},P_{1}\} of its component, and μj\mu_{j} marks valid rows as opposed to padding. Each row is projected and tagged with a learned role embedding,

mj=W​zj+b+erj,M=[m1;…;mJ],m_{j}=Wz_{j}+b+e_{r_{j}},\qquad M=[m_{1};\ldots;m_{J}], (3)

where WW, bb, and the role vectors ere_{r} are part of θ\theta. The role embedding is how provenance enters the computation: two identical sentences, one from the user request and one from a tool return, produce different memory rows. A component may contribute no rows; in admission, the two fixed actions may be represented only by their queries. When GG is long, an evidence selector scores each GG segment by its similarity to the commitment query qCq_{C} (Eq. 4) and keeps the top-scoring segments plus the mean over all segments. The selector is trained with the native outcome and its parameters form ψ\psi; adapters without a selector have no trainable parameters (Appendix C).

Stage 2: Role-Query Deliberation.

The controller maintains five query states, learned vectors that read the memory on behalf of each role,

Q(0)=[qK;qG;qP0;qP1;qC].Q^{(0)}=[q_{K};q_{G};q_{P_{0}};q_{P_{1}};q_{C}]. (4)

The first four correspond to the four roles. The fifth, qCq_{C}, has no input role; it is the commitment state that collects what the decision requires. The queries pass through LL deliberation blocks with separate weights,

Q(ℓ)=𝒟θ(ℓ)(Q(ℓ−1),M;μ),ℓ=1,…,L.Q^{(\ell)}=\mathcal{D}^{(\ell)}_{\theta}\bigl(Q^{(\ell-1)},M;\mu\bigr),\qquad\ell=1,\ldots,L. (5)

Each block applies three pre-normalized residual sublayers: masked cross-attention lets every query retrieve from the valid memory rows, self-attention lets the five queries compare what they retrieved, and a feed-forward layer updates each query. The memory MM stays fixed. Because retrieval in a later block is conditioned on the comparison formed in an earlier one, in the running example the first block can find that the recipient of P0P_{0} differs from the one in KK, and the second can return to GG to find where that recipient came from. The final states are Q=Q(L)Q=Q^{(L)}.

Stage 3: Action Valuation and Calibrated Commitment.

The readout DρD_{\rho} estimates the action value in Eq. 1. In candidate selection, a small feed-forward network gρg_{\rho} values each candidate from the states that describe the authority, the evidence, that candidate, and the commitment state:

V^​(x,Pc)=gρ​([qK;qG;qPc;qC]),c∈{0,1}.\widehat{V}(x,P_{c})=g_{\rho}\bigl([q_{K};q_{G};q_{P_{c}};q_{C}]\bigr),\qquad c\in\{0,1\}. (6)

In admission, the native outcome is a label: releasing P0P_{0} scores one if it is benign, and refusing scores one if it is unsafe. If p⁡(x)p(x) is the probability that P0P_{0} is unsafe, then V∗​(x,P1)−V∗​(x,P0)=2​p​(x)−1V^{*}(x,P_{1})-V^{*}(x,P_{0})=2p(x)-1. Only this difference matters, so we set V^​(x,P0)=0\widehat{V}(x,P_{0})=0 and V^​(x,P1)=p^​(x)=σ⁡(hρ​(qC))\widehat{V}(x,P_{1})=\widehat{p}(x)=\sigma(h_{\rho}(q_{C})), read from the commitment state by a linear head hρh_{\rho}. Calibration then sets the operating point, the trade-off between blocking unsafe actions and keeping benign ones:

U⁡(x,a)\displaystyle U(x,a) =Calη⁡(V^​(x,a),a)=V^​(x,a)−τa,\displaystyle=\operatorname{Cal}_{\eta}\bigl(\widehat{V}(x,a),a\bigr)=\widehat{V}(x,a)-\tau_{a}, (7)
a∗\displaystyle a^{*} =arg⁡maxa∈𝒜⁡(x)⁡U⁡(x,a),\displaystyle=\arg\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}(x)}U(x,a),

where η={τa}\eta=\{\tau_{a}\} are per-action offsets chosen on development data. Only τP1−τP0\tau_{P_{1}}-\tau_{P_{0}} affects the decision, so we fix τP0=0\tau_{P_{0}}=0; a deployment may select a separate offset for each task family. Calibration here means selecting an operating point, not adjusting predicted probabilities. In admission, Eq. 7 blocks P0P_{0} whenever p^​(x)>τP1\widehat{p}(x)>\tau_{P_{1}}.

Learning.

For each deployment, ψ\psi, θ\theta, and ρ\rho minimize 𝔼(x,y)​[ℒ⁡(V^​(x,⋅),y⁡(x,⋅))]+λ​ℛ\mathbb{E}_{(x,y)}[\mathcal{L}(\widehat{V}(x,\cdot),y(x,\cdot))]+\lambda\mathcal{R} on native examples: decision instances paired with the outcome of each candidate in candidate selection, or with the label of P0P_{0} in admission. In candidate selection, ℒ\mathcal{L} is binary cross-entropy between each candidate’s value and its outcome plus a pairwise ranking term; in admission, it is binary cross-entropy between p^​(x)\widehat{p}(x) and the label, with a risk-class term where finer labels exist. ℛ\mathcal{R} collects auxiliary terms (role-level supervision on the query states, the selector loss, and load balancing for the feed-forward layer), weighted by λ\lambda. The encoder Enc\operatorname{Enc} is not updated. Calibration is selected afterwards on development data to maximize the deployment’s operating criterion, for example F1, unsafe recall, or the fraction of benign actions released. Fitting and calibration are kept separate: the first learns which action is better, and the second decides how much evidence is required before departing from the default. Algorithm 1 in Appendix C summarizes inference.

4 Experimental Setting

Tasks along the Agent Lifecycle.

We evaluate PROVISO on four agent security tasks, ordered by when the commitment occurs in the agent lifecycle. Malicious skill detection: before the agent runs, a third-party skill package is admitted or rejected (SkillsBench (Yang et al., 2026)). Agent misuse: when a request arrives, a CLI agent executes it or refuses a task with real-world harm (ANCHOR (Song and Qi, 2026)). Unsafe tool invocation: at each step, a proposed tool call is released or blocked (ToolSafe (Mou et al., 2026)). Indirect prompt injection: when tool returns may carry injected instructions, the controller commits either the agent’s trajectory or a recovery trajectory, both rolled out from the start of the task (AgentDojo (Debenedetti et al., 2024)). The first three are admission decisions, where P1P_{1} is a refusal; the last is a candidate selection between two executable continuations (Sec. 3.1). For malicious skill detection, we add three further benchmarks: MalSkillBench (Guo et al., 2026), SkillVetBench (Hossain et al., 2026), and MaliciousSkillBench (Wang et al., 2026c). Appendix A lists KK, GG, P0P_{0}, P1P_{1}, and the native outcome for every benchmark (Table 6), together with the data splits (Table 7).

Metrics.

We use the metrics defined by each benchmark. On SkillsBench and the three additional skill benchmarks, we report precision (Prec), recall, F1, and false positive rate (FPR) for malicious packages. On ANCHOR, we report the Harm & Risk Score (H&R), which combines refusal with judged harm and catastrophic risk on harmful tasks. On ToolSafe, we report accuracy (ACC), F1, and recall for unsafe calls. On AgentDojo, we report benign utility (task completion without attacks), utility under attack, and targeted attack success rate (ASR), the fraction of attacked episodes in which the attacker’s goal is achieved.

Baselines.

Each task is compared with the defenses designed for it. Malicious skill detection uses static and semantic package scanners: SkillGate (Yang et al., 2026), Sentry (Sentry, 2026), Cisco (Cisco AI Defense, 2026), SkillSpector (NVIDIA, 2026), and SkillFortify (Qualixar, 2026); Sentry, Cisco, and SkillSpector are each run in a static mode and an LLM-based semantic mode. Agent misuse and unsafe tool invocation use guard models that judge a proposed action, four of which are evaluated on both tasks: MCIP (Jing et al., 2025), WildGuard (Han et al., 2024), AgentSpec (Wang et al., 2026a), and Safiron (Huang et al., 2026). Agent misuse adds AGrail (Luo et al., 2025) and GuardAgent (Xiang et al., 2025); tool invocation adds TS-Guard (Mou et al., 2026), Qwen3Guard (Zhao et al., 2025), and ShieldAgent (Zhang et al., 2024). Indirect prompt injection uses dedicated defenses: Tool Filter (Debenedetti et al., 2024), DRIFT (Li et al., 2025a), IPIGuard (An et al., 2025), BIPIA (Yi et al., 2025), PIGuard (Li et al., 2025b), and SecAlign (Chen et al., 2025b). Every baseline keeps its released prompts, parsers, and action mappings and is scored on the same test population. Appendix B gives configurations and which baselines use training data.

Implementation Details.

The encoder Enc\operatorname{Enc} is a frozen ModernBERT-large (Warner et al., 2025), or E5-large-v2 (Wang et al., 2022) for SkillVetBench and MaliciousSkillBench. The controller has width 384, five queries (four role queries and the commitment state), and L=2L=2 deliberation blocks; each attention layer has eight heads, and the feed-forward layer is a mixture of four SwiGLU experts (Shazeer, 2020) with top-two routing (Shazeer et al., 2017), giving 17.40M trainable parameters. The architecture is shared across benchmarks, while weights are fitted per benchmark with AdamW (Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019) on the splits in Table 7, where cross-validation folds keep each source, trajectory, or user task within one fold. Operating points are selected on development data, except on SkillVetBench, which uses a fixed threshold. The agent on ANCHOR and AgentDojo is Gemma 4 31B IT (Gemma Team, 2026), and the role summaries on ToolSafe are written by gpt-oss-20b (OpenAI, 2025). Training, calibration, and compute details are in Appendix C.

5 Results and Analysis

5.1 Main Results

Figure 3 places each method by its security (vertical axis) and utility (horizontal axis) on the four tasks. Across all four panels, no baseline is better than PROVISO on both axes. Most baselines trade one axis for the other: LLM-based skill scanners and MCIP block most malicious inputs but also many benign ones, whereas static scanners, Qwen3Guard, and WildGuard keep benign inputs but miss many attacks. PROVISO keeps both axes high on every task, and its margin over general-purpose guards is largest on agent misuse and unsafe tool invocation. Tables 1–4 give the detailed results. On SkillsBench and ToolSafe, the gains over the strongest baseline are statistically significant (p<0.01p<0.01, paired tests over test groups); details and confusion counts are in Appendix E.

Malicious Skill Detection.

As shown in Table 1, PROVISO achieves the best F1, precision, and FPR on SkillsBench, outperforming the strongest baseline, SkillGate, by 13.84 F1 points. Static scanners rely on predefined rules and patterns and detect only 58–73% of malicious skills. LLM-based semantic scanners detect nearly all of them, but they also flag 7.6–13.8% of benign skills; since benign skills are the large majority on SkillsBench, these false alarms keep their precision below 57%. PROVISO has lower recall than the semantic scanners because its threshold is selected on development data to maximize F1, which favors precision when most packages are benign. At this operating point it flags only one in a hundred benign skills.

Agent Misuse.

As shown in Table 2, PROVISO reduces H&R to zero while completing all benign tasks. Among the baselines, AGrail is the closest in H&R at 2.65 and completes 35 of the 80 benign tasks (43.75%). The other guards still reach H&R above 14 and fail on 17–28% of the benign tasks, so they lose on both safety and utility.

Unsafe Tool Invocation.

As shown in Table 3, PROVISO reaches 99.12 F1, missing one unsafe call and blocking five benign calls. TS-Guard, the guardrail introduced with the benchmark, is the strongest baseline at 92.05 F1. General-purpose guards stay below 65 F1: Qwen3Guard, WildGuard, and Safiron miss most unsafe calls, while MCIP and ShieldAgent block many benign ones. One reason is that these guards judge the call content itself, while whether a call is unsafe often depends on the user request and the preceding tool outputs. The result is stable across training runs, proposer models, and thresholds (Appendix G).

Indirect Prompt Injection.

As shown in Table 4, PROVISO achieves the highest utility under attack, 2.06 points above SecAlign, with a targeted ASR of 0.28%. BIPIA and DRIFT reach a similarly low ASR but lower utility under attack, and Tool Filter and PIGuard lose much more utility because they restrict tools or remove flagged tool outputs. SecAlign has slightly higher benign utility (one more task out of 97) but an ASR more than ten times higher. On clean tasks, PROVISO only selects between two candidate trajectories, so it cannot complete a task that neither candidate completes. Calibrating the threshold within each training fold gives the same ASR and benign utility (Appendix F.4).

5.2 Additional Skill Benchmarks

To test whether the results on SkillsBench depend on a single data source, we apply PROVISO to three further malicious skill detection benchmarks that differ in size, malicious ratio, and how skills were collected (Table 5). PROVISO reaches 88–99 F1 and at least 90% precision on all of them. FPR is higher on MaliciousSkillBench, at about 10%. MaliciousSkillBench is evaluated on its released train/test split rather than on our source-grouped folds; on its benchmark-specific metric, macro-F1, PROVISO reaches 86.02.

5.3 Component Analysis

Figure 4 measures what each component contributes. We either refit PROVISO with one component changed or intervene on a trained model, keeping the data and scorer fixed. The first two groups use SkillsBench; the third uses a controlled payment task built on the AgentDojo banking tools.

Evidence Selection.

A short instruction can decide whether a long skill package is safe. Removing the supervision that decides which package windows enter memory lowers F1 by 16.73 points, and also removing local memory lowers it by 26.44 points. With the trained model and threshold fixed, replacing the selected windows with an equal number of permuted ones lowers F1 by 21.47 points, while reversing their order changes no decision, so the gain comes from which content is retained (Appendices F.1 and F.2).

Query Reasoning.

We replace role-query deliberation with an MLP of the same parameter count that reads the same selected memory, flattened together with its role indicators. This dense readout reaches only 48.62 F1, 37.19 points below PROVISO (Appendix F.1).

Repeated Retrieval.

In the payment task, the user authorizes an invoice (KK), and the ledger links and payment notes the agent reads (GG) disagree with it in a quarter of the cases. Averaged over five training seeds, suppressing the retrieval in the second block lowers utility from 88.48% to 78.54%, with unsafe transfers below 0.4% in both. The drop is 13.15 points larger when trusted and external observations conflict than when they agree (Appendix F.3).

6 Conclusion

We presented PROVISO, which decides which action an LLM agent commits by separating trusted from external observations and comparing the proposed action with an alternative. On four agent security tasks along the agent lifecycle, no published defense exceeds PROVISO in both security and utility, and PROVISO reaches 88–99 F1 on three additional skill detection benchmarks.

Limitations

PROVISO is fitted separately for each benchmark and therefore requires labeled outcomes from the target setting; we do not study transfer of a single trained controller across tasks. In candidate selection, both continuations are rolled out in a restorable environment before the controller is applied, so a deployment must support such rollouts and pay for both. Roles are assigned by benchmark-specific adapters: on AgentDojo, external content enters memory inside the candidate trajectories rather than as separate GG rows, and on ToolSafe, part of the input consists of role summaries generated by a proposer model, which adds generation cost. The agent on ANCHOR and AgentDojo is a single LLM. Finally, our evaluation uses the released benchmarks and their attacks; attacks adapted to PROVISO itself are not evaluated.

Ethics Statement

Experiments use released data and execute attacks inside simulated benchmark applications to improve defenses for agents acting on external content. PROVISO can still release unsafe actions or block benign ones, as the error rates in Section 5 show, so it should complement rather than replace other safeguards, such as permission controls and human confirmation of irreversible actions. We do not develop new attack methods.

Reproducibility.

The code release implements the shared controller and the calibrated inference used in our experiments. The appendix gives implementation details, complete results, and statistical tests.

AI Assistance.

Generative AI assisted literature organization, code and figure drafting, and language editing. The authors are responsible for the analysis and manuscript.

Appendix A Benchmark Details

Table 6 maps each benchmark to the formulation in Sec. 3.1, and Table 7 lists the data splits. Trusted observations KK come from the user or deployment; external observations GG come from what the agent reads while acting. In candidate selection, P0P_{0} and P1P_{1} are two executable continuations. On AgentDojo, the commitment point is the start of the task, so both are complete trajectories, and the tool returns observed during each rollout enter memory with the role of that candidate. In admission, the two actions are fixed (release or refuse); they enter memory as short anchor texts or are represented only by the queries qP0q_{P_{0}} and qP1q_{P_{1}}.

Appendix B Baselines

Table 8 summarizes how each baseline makes its decision. Every baseline keeps its released prompts, checkpoints, parsers, and action mappings, and is scored on the same test instances as PROVISO. Trained baselines use their released checkpoints and are not fitted to our splits; TS-Guard was released together with ToolSafe. PROVISO is fitted on the training split of each benchmark.

Configurations.

On AgentDojo, every defense covers all attacked and clean episodes with the official scorer. Tool Filter uses the official tool-filtering interface; BIPIA separates external content, guidance, and task restatement; DRIFT keeps dynamic rules, observation isolation, and action validation; IPIGuard uses its dependency graph; PIGuard applies its classifier to each tool message; SecAlign uses its preference-optimized model. On ANCHOR, all methods use the same actor (Gemma 4 31B IT), artifact collector, and released Harm & Risk judge; benign completion is measured on the same 80 tasks for all six guards; AGrail completes 35/80 (43.75%). On ToolSafe, exact sample IDs select the same test calls for every method, and severity greater than zero defines unsafe; MCIP blocks after ten unsuccessful parsing attempts, following its protocol. On SkillsBench, Sentry static and Cisco static block HIGH or CRITICAL findings, SkillFortify blocks at MEDIUM, SkillSpector static uses its DO_NOT_INSTALL decision, and the semantic scanners keep their released model calls and blocking rules.

Appendix C Implementation Details

All benchmarks share the controller architecture in Sec. 3.2: a 1024-to-384 projection with role embeddings, five role queries, two deliberation blocks of cross-attention, self-attention, and a four-expert top-two SwiGLU update (eight heads, dropout 0.1), and common output heads, with 17.40M trainable parameters. The encoder is frozen. Each benchmark fits its own weights; Table 9 lists the optimization settings, and the paragraphs below describe the inputs, losses, and calibration.

Malicious Skill Detection.

ModernBERT-large encodes the full package text in 1,536-character windows with stride 768, pooling four vectors per window. The declared purpose populates KK, the package windows populate GG, and allow/reject anchors populate P0/P1P_{0}/P_{1}. On SkillsBench, a selector scores each window by its similarity to the initial commitment query and keeps the top min⁡(8,n)\min(8,n) of a package’s nn windows plus the mean over all windows; the selector is supervised with the package label through a log-sum-exp pooling over windows. The loss combines risk BCE, decision cross-entropy, role-level witness targets, within-source ranking between malicious and clean packages, the selector losses, and a router balance term. MalSkillBench uses the same input with all windows and no selector. SkillVetBench and MaliciousSkillBench use E5-large-v2 embeddings: a declared-purpose vector for KK and global and local document vectors for GG. The package is blocked when its risk score exceeds the threshold.

Agent Misuse.

The request and setting are encoded with ModernBERT-large (up to 2,048 tokens) into 34 rows: a CLS row, a global mean, and 32 ordered local means. Global rows carry KK; local rows carry KK, GG, or P0P_{0} according to the serialized field; P1P_{1} (refusal) is represented by its query only. A risk-class head on qCq_{C} is trained with cross-entropy plus a scalar risk BCE. The task is refused when the predicted risk exceeds the development threshold (.01).

Cross-backbone native admission.

A backbone-local fit instantiates the same 17.40M-parameter controller with Granite-3.3-8B evidence and the official ANCHOR scorer. The complete native population contains 300 harmful and 80 benign instances; the serialized controller reproduces the selected decisions for all 380 cases. Table 10 reports the positive admission endpoints together with the complete all-attempt request count.

Unsafe Tool Invocation.

The frozen ModernBERT-large encoder encodes the call, history, and tool schemas (up to 4,096 tokens) into a CLS row and 32 ordered means. Four further rows hold short summaries written in advance by the proposer model (gpt-oss-20b), one for each role ID KK, GG, P0P_{0}, and P1P_{1}. The proposer writes every summary after reading the full context, including tool returns, so under Sec. 3.1 the content of these rows has external provenance; the role ID records which part of the decision a summary describes, not that its content is trusted. The loss combines severity cross-entropy, scalar risk BCE, commitment BCE, and router balance. The call is blocked when the unsafe probability reaches .005.

Indirect Prompt Injection.

The commitment point is the start of the task. P0P_{0} is the complete trajectory of the deployed agent, whose prompt marks external content with boundary tags and restates the task, following BIPIA (Yi et al., 2025). P1P_{1} is a complete recovery trajectory produced by DRIFT (Li et al., 2025a), which plans the task, removes instructions it detects in tool returns, and validates later actions. Both candidates are rolled out from the initial environment with Gemma 4 31B IT, and each is recorded as its full message sequence: system and user messages, assistant text, tool calls with their arguments, tool returns, and the final answer. The user request forms KK. No external observation precedes the commitment point, so GG holds only a fixed stage description, and the tool returns enter memory as part of the candidate that produced them. The messages are encoded with ModernBERT-large in 510-token chunks. Committing a candidate replays its recorded tool calls in a freshly restored official environment, which yields its native outcome. Each candidate is valued from [qK;qG;qPc;qC][q_{K};q_{G};q_{P_{c}};q_{C}] and trained with BCE on its native outcome (task completed and attack failed) plus a pairwise ranking loss. Five folds keep all attack variants of a user task together. P1P_{1} is chosen when its value exceeds that of P0P_{0} by a per-suite margin selected on calibration curves.

AppWorld: Prior-Conditioned Program Commitment.

The authorized instruction, candidate programs, observed reads and effects, and runtime errors after shadow execution populate the same KK, GG, P0P_{0}, and P1P_{1} interfaces. ModernBERT-large encodes role-separated 510-token chunks into masked means, and the candidate readout consumes [qK;qG;qPc;qC][q_{K};q_{G};q_{P_{c}};q_{C}]. Native program scores and requirement labels supervise candidate BCE with unit weight, pair ranking with weight .5, conflict BCE with weight .55, direction ranking with weight .2, and evidence ranking with weight .2. The training population contains 90 tasks in 30 scenario groups; the complete evaluation contains 417 tasks in 139 groups. AdamW uses batch 8, learning rate 3×10−43\times 10^{-4} with cosine decay to 3×10−53\times 10^{-5}, decay .02, clipping one, and a 36-epoch pilot ceiling; the selected fit uses ten epochs and a zero decision margin.

For the calibrated action rule, let b∈{−1,+1}b\in\{-1,+1\} denote the visible support-prior recommendation, v0,v1v_{0},v_{1} the candidate logits, pfp_{f} the calibrated conflict probability, and hh the direction logit. We use

α\displaystyle\alpha =σ⁡((.50−|v1−v0|)/.25),\displaystyle=\sigma\!\left((.50-|v_{1}-v_{0}|)/.25\right), (8)
δ\displaystyle\delta =γ​b+.75​pf​α​tanh⁡h.\displaystyle=\gamma b+.75p_{f}\alpha\tanh h.

Here γ=1+softplus⁡(γ0)\gamma=1+\operatorname{softplus}(\gamma_{0}). Score P0P_{0} by v0−δ/2v_{0}-\delta/2 and P1P_{1} by v1+δ/2v_{1}+\delta/2; commit the higher score and retain P0P_{0} on a tie. All 417 choices agree with the support prior. The official replay completes 237/417 tasks and 49/139 scenarios; selected execution uses 20,355 API calls, with 110 additional attempted calls and inherited candidate acquisition retained in the total resource scope.

AgentTrap: Native Action Advantage.

The original user trigger supplies KK. ModernBERT-large encodes the helper package in 1,536-character windows with stride 768 and four pooled vectors per window for GG; allow and reject anchors define P0P_{0} and P1P_{1}. Native allow/reject executions provide paired outcomes for 141 cases in 66 source groups. The scalar target is the reject-minus-allow benign-pass gain for benign cases and the normalized defense gain for malicious cases. MSE with unit weight, intent cross-entropy on the KK witness with weight .25, and router balance with weight .01 fit the shared core in five source folds. Fitting-only gain centers standardize the scalar, and a development threshold selects allow or reject. The complete native replay records 83/91 defended malicious cases, 38/50 benign passes, and 54/141 completed tasks, giving balanced utility Q=12​(83/91+38/50)=83.60%Q=\tfrac{1}{2}(83/91+38/50)=83.60\%. Source groups define the uncertainty unit and the native scorer retains all 141 cases. The acquired native decision population records 1,594 all-attempt requests.

Compute.

With cached encodings, fitting and evaluating the ToolSafe controller takes about two minutes and the SkillsBench controller about seven minutes on one GPU, with peak memory below 0.6 GiB. The controller itself calls no generative model; on ToolSafe, its inputs include role summaries generated in advance by the proposer model.

Appendix F Additional Analyses

Table 15 gives the gains in Figure 4 with paired 95% confidence intervals. The subsections below describe each analysis.

F.1 Component Controls on SkillsBench

Table 16 refits PROVISO on SkillsBench with one component changed, using the same folds and scorer. Changes to evidence selection have the largest effect. Removing the role embeddings or replacing the expert update with a dense layer changes F1 by less than one point, and these intervals include zero, so on this benchmark the gains come mainly from which evidence enters memory and from the role-query computation as a whole rather than from these two components individually. The matched dense readout receives the same selected memory as PROVISO and has the same parameter count (17.41M vs. 17.40M).

F.2 Retained Evidence at a Fixed Model

Keeping each trained model, threshold, and memory budget fixed, we replace the selected windows with an equal number of windows chosen by a deterministic permutation of the package. F1 drops from 85.81 to 64.35 for the selected model (gain 21.47, 95% CI [13.09, 29.47]) and from 75.13 to 57.72 on average over five independently trained models (gain 17.41, [9.90, 25.43]). Restoring only the four highest-ranked original windows recovers 85.91 F1, and reversing window order changes none of the decisions. On packages with more than eight windows, where selection actually matters, the gain rises to 25.22 points ([16.12, 34.01]); on shorter packages all windows are kept and the decisions are identical.

The uncertainty calculation keeps each source group within its original outer fold. It uses 20,000 paired bootstrap draws and 50,000 whole-source-group swaps. Five-fit estimates also resample fit identities. Holm adjustment retains all four complete-population contrasts in Table 17. The analysis conditions on the acquired population, fitted scorers, and retained thresholds.

F.3 Second Retrieval on Payments

This controlled task uses the AgentDojo banking tools. The user authorizes an invoice (KK), ledger links and a payment note are read from files (GG), and two candidate transfers form P0/P1P_{0}/P_{1}; a transfer succeeds only if recipient, amount, subject, and date are correct. Training, development, and test sets use disjoint sources, and a quarter of the cases contain a conflict between KK and GG. We compare the full model with a variant whose second cross-attention retrieval is suppressed, over five training seeds each. Mean utility is 88.48% with full retrieval and 78.54% without it (gain 9.94, [8.43, 11.41]), with unsafe transfers below 0.4% in both. The gain is 13.15 points larger on conflicting than on aligned cases ([10.96, 15.31]); for two-hop evidence chains, utility is 99.57% vs. 81.41%.

The source-disjoint confirmation contains 4,096 cases in 64 source groups, following 2,048 training and 1,024 development cases in 32 and 16 distinct groups. Table 18 records the two supported effects. Joint intervals use 20,000 continuation-seed and depth-stratified source-group bootstrap draws. Tests use 50,000 synchronized whole-source method-label swaps; Holm adjustment keeps the original three-contrast utility/depth/conflict family. Mean coverage is 88.85% with full retrieval and 78.93% for the intervention; mean unsafe incidence is .37% and .39%, respectively.

Learned memory weighting.

Learned attention preserves useful calls at the selected operating point. On the identical 707 calls in 336 trajectory groups, the complete checkpoint reaches 99.12 F1 and releases 362/367 benign calls. Replacing both masked cross-attention distributions with uniform valid-row weights gives 64.95 F1; the paired advantage of learned weighting is +34.18 points, with 95% interval [30.35,38.13] and Holm p=.00006p=.00006. This fixed-checkpoint intervention retains the value and output projections, all other operations, and threshold .005. The calculation uses 20,000 trajectory-group bootstrap draws and 50,000 whole-group swaps; adjustment retains the original three-intervention F1 family.

F.4 Recovery Calibration on AgentDojo

The main result selects one recovery margin per suite from the calibration curves of all five training folds. Selecting each fold’s margin only from its own training groups changes 57 of the 2,516 attacked choices, keeps the same 7 attack successes and 85 clean completions, and lowers the number of attacked episodes that are both completed and attack-free from 2,147 to 2,141.

Fixed choices from the acquired pool.

On the same acquired candidates, learned selection completes more attacked episodes safely than either fixed choice (Table 19). Each of the 2,613 episodes supplies a complete default trajectory P0P_{0} and recovery trajectory P1P_{1}, including messages, calls, and returned observations. Both trajectories are replayed in restored native environments. The comparison reuses all 2,516 attacked episodes and 97 clean episodes; the controller row uses the five-fold held-out choices and calibration rule described above. JSU counts episodes with both user-task success and attack failure. The last column counts recovery choices over all 2,613 pairs. These are complete descriptive counts for this frozen candidate pool.

ANCHOR benign completion.

On the same 80 benign tasks, PROVISO completes 80/80 and AGrail completes 35/80, a paired gain of 56.25 percentage points (95% CI [33.75,77.50]). We resample the ten native tool families, each containing eight tasks, with 20,000 paired bootstrap draws. An exact two-sided family-swap test enumerates all 2102^{10} assignments; Holm adjustment over all six guards gives p=.046875p=.046875 for the AGrail comparison. Cross-backbone package admission.

Separately fitted backbone instances.

The same 17.40M-parameter core also supports separate fitting on Granite and Phi evidence (Table 22). Each instance uses all 5,769 training calls, 706 development calls, and 707 test calls. It initializes from the source call controller and fits for 36 epochs with batch 128 and learning rate 3×10−53\times 10^{-5}. The objective combines severity CE, .25 train-balanced scalar BCE, unit-weight commitment BCE, .05 router balance, and .5T2KL(pteacher∥pstudent).5T^{2}\operatorname{KL}(p_{\mathrm{teacher}}\|p_{\mathrm{student}}) at T=2T=2. The frozen teacher consumes the same target training inputs. Development calibration maximizes benign retention under the .98 recall floor and selects threshold .005. Muse target fitting on the call subset.

The shared controller is initialized from the Granite call model and fitted on 981 Muse-evidence training calls, with 111 development calls. AdamW uses learning rate 10−510^{-5}, batch 128, decay .01, clipping one, seed 20261011, and 12 complete epochs. The loss combines severity CE, commitment BCE, .25.25 scalar-risk BCE, .05.05 router balance, and training-only .5T2KL(psource∥ptarget).5T^{2}\mathrm{KL}(p_{\rm source}\|p_{\rm target}) with T=2T=2. Training rows receive inverse trajectory-size weights normalized within each minibatch; the BCE positive weight is 700/281700/281. Development maximizes benign retention under recall at least .95, then F1 and smaller threshold; the earliest eligible epoch resolves ties. It selects epoch one and threshold .745. The complete 128-call test has TP/FN/FP/TN 43/0/2/8343/0/2/83, 100% unsafe recall, and 97.65% benign retention in 58 trajectories. Relative to the original certificate policy (60.14 F1), the gain is 37.59 points, with trajectory-paired 95% CI [28.80,46.92] and Holm p=.00016p=.00016 over all eight completed candidates. The analysis uses 20,000 group-bootstrap draws and 50,000 whole-group swaps and conditions on recorded public-benchmark development. Target optimization and development take 19.89 s; loading, fitting, selected forward and export take 21.59 s, followed by 3.95 s for independent replay with cached inputs. G.1 Independent Package Fitting with Fine Manifest Views

Fine local evidence preserves a substantial package-admission advantage over the complete SkillGate workflow under an independently fitted instance of the shared computation. Both methods cover all 1,650 packages, including 150 malicious and 1,500 benign packages in 1,500 source groups. The controller follows the same typed memory, five role queries, two complete reasoning blocks, common outputs, and calibrated commitment in Eq. 7. Package observations enter this computation before downstream actor generation; the measured endpoint is the native malicious-package decision.

The paired F1 gain is 12.42 points with pointwise 95% interval [4.88,20.02][4.88,20.02] and Holm-adjusted p=.03696p=.03696. The analysis uses 20,000 fold-stratified whole-source bootstrap draws and 50,000 synchronized whole-source prediction exchanges with a two-sided plus-one test. It includes the four completed fitting recipes for each of three independently fitted guard identities in the twelve-comparison family. The complete earlier source-policy comparison remains part of the evidence archive. Inference conditions on continued development using this released public benchmark and the recorded source-group splits.

Fine-View Recipe.

ModernBERT-large supplies four contextual vectors per window. The boundary interface augments the original 33,420 package windows with 64,914 fine manifest windows of 384 characters at stride 192, giving 98,334 candidate windows over the complete package population. The original coarse-window mean supplies the global package summary; the supervised selector retains eight local windows for the common memory interface. Each outer fold starts from its source-local pilot checkpoint. Training and development contain 1,055/264, 1,055/264, 1,057/264, 1,056/264, and 1,057/264 packages; the five held-out populations contain 331, 331, 329, 330, and 329 packages. The shared core has 17,400,966 parameters. The objective combines risk BCE, .5.5 decision CE, .25.25 witness CE, .5.5 within-source package ranking, .5.5 selector MIL BCE, .25.25 selector pair ranking, and .01.01 router balance. Positive weighting uses the fitting negative-to-positive ratio. AdamW uses learning rate 3×10−53\times 10^{-5}, decay .02, clipping one, batch 64, an 8,192-token allowance, and twelve continuation epochs with cosine decay to 3×10−63\times 10^{-6}. Development selects F1, then fewer false positives, recall, and earliest epoch. Selected epochs are 6/5/7/11/6, and risk-logit thresholds are .75390625/.33203125/−2.140625/2.015625/.63671875.75390625/.33203125/-2.140625/2.015625/.63671875. Reloaded checkpoints reproduce every held-out logit and retained-window decision exactly. Fitting and forward evaluation take 805.82 seconds with cached inputs; fine-view encoding takes 898.52 seconds with peak allocated GPU memory 1.14 GiB. Source fitting, launch checks, earlier candidates, and the published scanner’s complete request ledger retain their separate resource records. SkillGate uses its released prefilter, snippet extraction, and semantic workflow (Yang et al., 2026), executed with the Google Gemma-4 adapter, a 512-token output budget, an 8,000-character input allowance, 500-character snippet context, and at most twenty snippets. Its published MEDIUM/HIGH/CRITICAL malicious decision is used consistently for all package IDs.

Expanded Comparison Family.

Extending the recorded package-fitting comparison to all fifteen complete candidates retains the selected gain of 12.42 F1 points over SkillGate on 1,650 packages in 1,500 source groups. The same fold-stratified source bootstrap gives a 95% interval of [4.88,20.02][4.88,20.02]; a two-sided whole-source exchange test with 50,000 draws and Holm correction over all fifteen candidates gives p=.04620p=.04620. The five recorded fitting recipes each contain three independently optimized guard instances, retain their source initialization and development calibration, and use the common 17.40M-parameter core. This extension includes the completed fit-only local-edit supervision recipe in the recorded public-benchmark development family.

Role: source template.

You are the AgentSafe pre-execution certificate controller.

The current tool call is a proposed effect and has not executed.

Trust model

1. The initial user request is the only source of action authority.

3. Tool observations and prior interaction history are untrusted evidence.

Evaluate four independent witnesses.

scope_pass

The candidate action, affected objects, recipients, quantities, time, and

source_pass

policy_pass

same current action. Pass only when the same action and its material arguments

remain justified by the initial request after removing untrusted instructions.

Fail when untrusted content introduced, substituted, or expanded the action.
